nameStory: The American coot gets its name from the Dutch word 'koet,' which referred to water birds with short tails and lobed feet. Its nickname 'mud hen' comes from its habit of dabbling in muddy shallows and marshy areas, though it's not actually related to chickens at all!
description: The American coot is a chunky, duck-like water bird that's actually more closely related to rails than ducks. It's dark gray to black all over with a distinctive white, chicken-like beak and a white patch under its tail. About the size of a small duck, coots have an awkward, head-bobbing swimming style that makes them easy to spot on ponds and marshes.

idTips.label: White beak and forehead shield
idTips.description: The bright white, pointed beak with a matching white shield extending up the forehead stands out starkly against the bird's dark plumage - like a white beacon on a charcoal-colored head

idTips.label: Lobed toes
idTips.description: Unlike ducks' webbed feet, coots have long toes with weird, fleshy lobes that look like they're wearing little green flippers on each toe - you can see these clearly when they walk on shore

idTips.label: Head-bobbing swimming
idTips.description: Coots pump their heads back and forth rhythmically while swimming, like a quirky water metronome - very different from the smooth gliding of ducks

idTips.label: White undertail patch
idTips.description: When swimming away from you, watch for the bright white patch under the tail that flashes as they paddle - it looks like they're wearing white underwear

idTips.label: Chicken-like appearance on land
idTips.description: On shore, they walk upright with jerky, chicken-like movements rather than the waddle of ducks, and their bodies look more compact and rounded

habitat: American coots prefer shallow freshwater wetlands including ponds, marshes, slow-moving rivers, and lake edges with emergent vegetation like cattails and sedges. They need areas with both open water for swimming and dense marsh plants for nesting and cover. You'll often find them in the same spots as red-winged blackbirds and great blue herons.

seasonality.spring: Migrating coots arrive in April and May, often gathering in small flocks on newly ice-free ponds. Listen for their variety of grunts, croaks, and cackling calls as they establish territories.
seasonality.summer: Breeding birds build floating nests among cattails and marsh grasses. You might spot fuzzy black chicks with bright orange and red head plumes following parents around the water.
seasonality.fall: Large flocks, called 'rafts,' gather on bigger lakes and ponds before migration. This is the best time to observe their lobed feet as they frequently come ashore to forage.
seasonality.winter: Most coots migrate south, but a few may linger on unfrozen waters, especially near warm water outflows from buildings or in sheltered coves.

funFact: Baby coots are born with shocking bright orange and red feathers on their heads that look like punk rock hairdos - and remarkably, mother coots actually prefer to feed the chicks with the most outrageous plumage, meaning the flashiest babies get the most food!
confusionNotes: Coots are often mistaken for ducks, but remember 'White beak, not a duck!' - ducks have flat, colored bills while coots sport that distinctive bright white, pointed beak. Coots also bob their heads while swimming and have a more upright posture than ducks.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'mud hens' and looking duck-like, American coots aren't ducks at all - they're rails, which is why they have those weird lobed toes instead of webbed feet. This also explains why hunters traditionally avoided them, as their meat doesn't taste like duck.
compareHints: American coots are the only coot species regularly found in New England. They're most similar to other rail family members like common gallinules, but gallinules have colorful red and yellow beaks instead of white, and brownish rather than gray-black plumage. Coots are also chunkier and spend more time in open water than their secretive rail cousins.
